title: The Pacific Is a Mess of Hurricanes
summary: If you could look down at the Pacific Ocean right now, you’d see three hurricanes spinning in a row, between 15 and 20 degrees north. Furthest east is Polo, an unusually strong hurricane that has been churning off the southern coast of Mexico for nearly a week. To its west, Odalys, once a Category 4...
content:
If you could look down at the Pacific Ocean right now, you’d see three hurricanes spinning in a row, between 15 and 20 degrees north. Furthest east is Polo, an unusually strong hurricane that has been churning off the southern coast of Mexico for nearly a week. To its west, Odalys, once a Category 4 hurricane, is slowly weakening in the open ocean. In the central Pacific, Hurricane Nolo has reached Category 2 status and has crept about 145 miles off the coast of Hawaii’s Big Island, where it’s expected to bring up to 25 inches of rain, potentially causing flooding and landslides. The ocean is a mess of hurricanes, and it’s not the first time this season.

Just last month, four storms formed across the Pacific over a 12-day period. Two of them, Hurricane Lala and Tropical Storm Moke, came dangerously close to Hawaii. Driven by an exceptional El Niño event, these tropical storms have increased in frequency compared with an average year. Typically, at this point in the season, 12 tropical storms would have formed in the eastern Pacific, Michael Brennan, the director of the National Hurricane Center, told me. This year, there have already been 17.

Of the storms in the Pacific now, Polo, which has wobbled between Category 4 and 5, is the monster, and it will likely bring catastrophic damage when it makes landfall on Monday. The warm water temperatures associated with El Niño increase the likelihood of stronger storms, and this year’s event is shaping up to be one of the most dramatic on record. “El Niño is the ‘great nudger’ of weather systems around the planet,” Michelle L’Heureux, who leads the El Niño–Southern Oscillation team at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Climate Prediction Center, wrote in an email. “Very strong El Niños are often able to nudge more.”

Warmer waters also mean that the area where a storm can form expands. Storms tend to show up in the region where Polo is lingering, Brennan said, and generally, by the time they reach the central part of the ocean, near Hawaii, they weaken. But this year, waters in the central Pacific are more than 3 degrees Celsius warmer than usual, allowing hurricanes such as Nolo to form south of the islands and much closer to them. When I asked Brennan how abnormal this was—I’d seen others calling this a historic hurricane season—he said that a season like this comes around every decade or so. Still, it’s a big one.

Nolo is only the latest in a string of disasters that the island of Hawaii has endured this year. In January, the Kilauea volcano erupted for eight hours, and blanketed communities on the island with rocks and ash. Then, back-to-back Kona lows, a type of seasonal cyclone, brought historic flooding in March. Two months later, a 6.0-magnitude earthquake shook the island and damaged nearly 150 homes. In mid-August, Hurricane Lala, a Category 1 storm, dumped some 30 inches of rain on parts of the Big Island without making landfall.

David Ho, a professor of oceanography at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, was at home in Honolulu when Lala hit. His neighborhood flooded, and he was one of 200,000 electricity customers across the state who lost power. More than 200 homes and an estimated $67 million worth of public infrastructure were damaged, according to the Hawaii Emergency Management Agency. “We have a lot of houses that were built before the building codes were modernized,” Ho told me. “So once in a while, you have roofs that just fly away.”

Weeks later, many people, especially those in rural areas with limited access to groceries, are still feeling Lala’s lingering effects. “We always talk about the importance of being prepared, and you want to have three weeks of food supply and everything,” Janice Ikeda, the CEO of the nonprofit Vibrant Hawaii, told me. “Well, we don’t have that anymore, because it got wiped out.” (The state reissued Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits to more than 65,000 households after the storm.) The damage and losses the island suffered from Lala only make lives and infrastructure more vulnerable in the face of Nolo.

For even one storm to skirt that close to Hawaii would have been an event: The Pacific Ocean is big enough, and the Hawaiian Islands are small enough, that most hurricanes roll by at a much greater distance. But earlier this month, another storm, Lowell, approached the western part of the state, near Kauai and Niihau, pushing hurricane-strength winds and waves ashore. More than 90 percent of utility customers in Kauai lost power.

Nolo likely won’t be a repeat of Lala or Lowell, because it is farther out and should remain 100 miles from the coast, Brennan said. Even so, the island could see more than two feet of rain, coastal flooding, and high surf. The hurricane season doesn’t end for another two months, and the effect of El Niño is likely to only get stronger, according to NOAA’s current predictions. Before the year is through, the “great nudger” will likely hurl more hurricanes Hawaii’s way.

In the Atlantic, the nudge is working in the opposite direction: El Niño generates strong wind shears, which make it hard for hurricanes to form. September should mark the peak of the Atlantic hurricane season, Allison Wing, an associate professor of atmospheric science at Florida State University, told me. Nearly four months into hurricane season, no hurricanes have appeared, and none are on the horizon.

title: What Israel Knew Before October 7
summary: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket CastsLess than two weeks before October 7, 2023, Egypt’s top spy flew to Israel to deliver a dire warning: Hamas appeared to be mobilizing for a major attack. According to officials who spoke with the Atlantic staff writer Vivian...
content:
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts

Less than two weeks before October 7, 2023, Egypt’s top spy flew to Israel to deliver a dire warning: Hamas appeared to be mobilizing for a major attack. According to officials who spoke with the Atlantic staff writer Vivian Salama, Cairo’s intelligence chief recommended that the Israeli government offer economic concessions to Hamas in order to avert conflict. What Israeli officials did with that warning remains an open question three years after the most devastating surprise attack in the country’s history. On this episode of Radio Atlantic, Salama says officials from seven different countries told her that the visit should have set off alarms across the top ranks of the Israeli government.

The following is a transcript of the episode:

Adam Harris:  I’m Adam Harris, and I’m here in the PBS studios of Washington Week With The Atlantic for a special taping of Radio Atlantic, with Atlantic staff writer Vivian Salama. Vivian, thank you so much for joining me. You have some new, exclusive reporting, and the headline of the story is “Egypt’s Warning to Israel.” It’s about the October 7th attack. What did you find out about the October 7th attack?

Vivian Salama: Adam, we’re coming up on the third anniversary of the tragic attacks of October 7th, and I set out several months ago to try to understand exactly what was known. I was starting to get bits and pieces of information from sources about possible warnings that came in advance of it—easy to dismiss on its face because Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and most of his government have denied that there were prior warnings ahead of the tragedy.

But the more I looked into it and the more people I talked to, I realized a very peculiar incident that happened exactly on September 26th, 2023. And the reason this date was so significant and really stood out is because that was the day that the government held a very large 50th-anniversary commemoration of the Yom Kippur War: the war 50 years ago when, ironically, Egypt and Syria launched a surprise attack on Israel. And the whole premise of his speech was essentially that we need to be prepared, that we wouldn’t turn a blind eye to the threats around us and to our adversaries.

All the while, about two hours prior to Netanyahu taking the stage, a small Cessna jet arrived in Ben-Gurion Airport about 30 miles away from where Bibi was talking. I really had to dig deep and work for months to try to figure out who this Cessna belonged to. There had been some rumors and some tips that it belonged to the Egyptian security chief, the intelligence chief. But I really had to actually connect those dots and go down rabbit holes to try to really confirm that this was his plane; the flight plan was Cairo to Ben-Gurion. And what we found from multiple, multiple applications, but also the Israeli flight logs which we later discovered, is that that plane landed early that morning, kinda tucked away in this very restricted area at Ben-Gurion Airport, and stayed for about 67 minutes, according to the Israeli flight log. That is a very short time.

And through multiple sources, and I’m talking to people in Israel, in Egypt, across the Arab world, in Europe, and the United States, I managed to confirm that he was on that plane, the Egyptian intelligence chief. His name is Abbas Kamel. He’s now the former chief. He was there, and he came with a very ominous message of danger in Gaza. And so he met with security officials in the Israeli government, some senior officials, and essentially conveyed to them what they saw, which was that there was mobilization for an unprecedented attack of some kind. He didn’t know the date. He didn’t know the mode of attack. But he knew that the situation was so grave. And for him to go to Israel for 67 minutes to deliver a message—that alone signified that the situation was so urgent and so grave. And so the question then became: What happened with the message? Typically something like this—just the sheer presence of the Egyptian intelligence chief would send off red flags across the Israeli government. My sources tell me that after Netanyahu finished his speech at the Yom Kippur ceremony, he went into a classified meeting. Some believe that he would’ve gotten the warning then; however, the Netanyahu government refused to answer my questions, and so it remains unclear if those warnings made it to him or not. Countless Israeli officials I talked to said, There is no world—literally, that’s a direct quote—There is no world in which the Egyptian spy chief comes to Israel for an hour to deliver a message, where likely the Egyptian president commissioned him to go, and Bibi doesn't know about that. And so the question then became: What more did they know? It seems clear, and even through U.S. officials, I later confirmed, that they had multiple warnings from the Egyptians. But in particular, within that two-week time frame of the October 7th attack, you had the visit from Abbas Kamel to Israel. You also had two written cables that went to them warning them of a possible attack. And so all of this is a collective body of evidence that really signaled that there was trouble brewing right on Israel’s doorstep.

Harris: You’ve mentioned that the prime minister had denied that there were warnings before. Were there other warnings in addition to these that you’ve mentioned, that we have confirmed? Or were these the only warnings?

Salama: So through months of investigating this, I was able to determine that the United Arab Emirates’ president, Mohamed bin Zayed, also picked up the phone probably the same day or around the same time as Abbas Kamel visited Israel. Now, that story, to the credit of Haaretz, the newspaper in Israel, they got that element of it out a couple of weeks ago and were able to report it. I have independently confirmed that the story’s absolutely correct. And my understanding through all my sources that I talked to is that that phone call was actually largely inspired by the Egyptian intelligence he received. I want to emphasize that when it comes to Gaza, there are two countries that basically have eyes on it, and that is Israel and Egypt. They both border Gaza. They have sources within the Strip, and they follow it very closely because both countries, despite all their differences, really view Hamas’s activity within the Strip as a security threat to both of their countries. And so they do work very closely on intelligence sharing when it comes to Gaza. And so for the Egyptian intel chief to travel to Israel—that is someone who knows what he’s talking about. But it also appears that Egypt dispersed that intelligence throughout the region, that officials in the region knew he traveled to Israel as well. And MBZ, Mohamed bin Zayed, was so disturbed by the findings he was hearing, both from the Egyptians and from his own Palestinian sources, that he picked up the phone and called Netanyahu directly. And so again, a growing body of evidence that signals the fact that the Netanyahu government had warnings that should have at least sent off some signals or mobilized the Israeli military in a way to reinforce that border with Gaza.

Harris: I want to talk about Israel in the current, present day. They have a really big election coming up. What does this mean for the upcoming election? How might this impact the upcoming election?

Salama: So just to emphasize, Benjamin Netanyahu served as prime minister longer than anyone else in Israel’s history. He has come and gone, but he has been serving for quite some time and is increasingly a very polarizing figure in Israeli society. In fact, in the lead-up to 2023—and this is something I get into in the story—Israelis were consumed by domestic issues regarding some of Benjamin Netanyahu’s more controversial moves. Obviously, after October 7th, one of the biggest matters that has consumed the Israeli public is the security issues, and particularly what happened on October 7th and whether or not his government has handled that correctly. One of the big things that one of his prime adversaries or his political opponents, Gadi Eisenkot—who used to be the IDF’s chief of staff before October 7th; he left—has been calling for is an independent state inquiry. And those calls have really been growing in the public in Israel, where they want something similar to, I should mention, what was done during the Yom Kippur War 50 years prior, where they did launch an independent state inquiry into the intelligence failures and the military failures that took place then. But Netanyahu and his government have rejected it. They’ve proposed as an alternative a sort of politically appointed inquiry that would be what the opposition calls very orchestrated. And so they’ve really pushed back, and the opposition in particular has refused to take part in that. And so this is a very contentious issue. Israeli officials, the Israeli public—I’ve spoken to bereaved families as part of this investigation, and they feel that accountability has just never happened when it comes to this. This is the largest tragedy in modern Israel, and certainly the largest attack on Jews since the Holocaust. And Israelis keep saying, If this was such a trauma, and we acknowledge collectively that this was such a trauma for our country, then why are we not taking time to dig into what happened? And obviously, we know it wasn’t just a trauma for the Israelis; 1,200 Israelis killed that day on October 7th in a multi-pronged attack by Hamas. But obviously, the war in Gaza that followed as well, where more than 73,000 Palestinians were killed in Gaza. In both cases, most of them were civilians. So over the past three years, you increasingly see not just Israelis demanding accountability, but all over the world, a demand for accountability on the war that followed with obviously the death of tens of thousands of civilians being a flash point all over the world.

Harris: Well, Vivian, thank you so much for your reporting, and thank you for sharing with us. Thanks for joining us for this bonus episode of Radio Atlantic. You can read Vivian’s full story at theatlantic.com.

title: How to Define the Fuzzy Phases of Life
summary: This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight. Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning.When, exactly, does middle age begin and end? This past summer, my colleague Julie Beck tried to figu...
content:
This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight. Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning.

When, exactly, does middle age begin and end? This past summer, my colleague Julie Beck tried to figure it out. Public opinion didn’t exactly offer a consensus: “In one survey, the median response put middle age as lasting from 40 to 60,” Beck writes. But The Wall Street Journal also reported a few years ago that 20 percent of people ages 25 to 34 claim they feel middle-aged. People tend to think about the term in relation to the age they currently are, Beck writes. “The older people are, the later they tend to think middle age starts and ends.”

At a certain point in her quest to define the exact contours of middle age, “I started losing my grip a little,” Beck writes. The numbers were nearly impossible to pin down, and “ultimately, middle age might be better understood as a feeling that creeps up on you than as a clear turning point.”

“It’s a time of life that is often both exhausting and fulfilling,” Beck notes: “when you’ve lived enough life to have learned some lessons, and also have plenty of time ahead of you to make changes.” That feeling may show up at 35, or 45, or 65. Perhaps all that matters is what we do with it when it arrives.

PS

Courtesy of Eilene L.

“I went on a Maui vacation in April 2026” and “spied this Gold Dust Gecko on the opening of a trash can,” Eilene L., 64, from Durango, Colorado, writes. “He was quite unperturbed as I took several close-up photos. The trash can opening proved to be an excellent backdrop to make the reptile stand out. Who’d have thought?”

I’ll continue to feature your responses in the coming weeks.

— Isabel

title: Xi’s Visit to Washington

content:
Editor’s Note: Washington Week With The Atlantic is a partnership between NewsHour Productions, WETA, and The Atlantic airing every Friday on PBS stations nationwide. Check your local listings, watch full episodes here, or listen to the weekly podcast here.

Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington, D.C., this week for a state visit. Panelists on Washington Week With The Atlantic joined to discuss what Xi’s conversations with President Trump reveal about trade, AI, the war with Iran, and more.

It seemed almost as if Xi and Trump “were in two different places,” Adam Harris, the host of Radio Atlantic said last night. “Trump likes to move fast and negotiate and say, We’re going to get a deal done right now, and China is saying, Well, we’re still trying to thaw this relationship that has been sort of tense.”

Joining the editor in chief of The Atlantic, Jeffrey Goldberg, to discuss this and more: Peter Baker, a chief White House correspondent at The New York Times; Susan Glasser, a staff writer at The New Yorker; Harris; Vivian Salama, a staff writer at The Atlantic.

Watch the full episode here.

title: Modern Media Weaken the Presidency
summary: Donald Trump’s second term represents a new, bolder version of the “imperial presidency” that many feared half a century ago. Trump prefers a maximalist approach to presidential power. And the Supreme Court, by granting presidents immunity from most prosecution and subduing what were once thought of...
content:
Donald Trump’s second term represents a new, bolder version of the “imperial presidency” that many feared half a century ago. Trump prefers a maximalist approach to presidential power. And the Supreme Court, by granting presidents immunity from most prosecution and subduing what were once thought of as independent agencies, has lent him some support.

One might assume that the media have done so as well, albeit inadvertently—that as the news business has become weaker, the presidency has become stronger. Most local newspapers have collapsed in the hands of hedge funds and private equity; advertising has been gobbled up by digital platforms; tens of thousands of journalists have lost their job. Trump has used the press to his political advantage, often appearing omnipresent and dominant in the news. Last week, he banned CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House because of their critical coverage, in a seeming show of force.

A judge has already blocked that legally dubious ban. What’s more, a closer look at the changes that have swept through the news business this century reveals that their tendency is to weaken the presidency, undermining Trump’s attempts to exert control. Individual journalists and publications continue to provide an important check on the president. Other structural forces in the industry have made the effective exercise of presidential power more difficult.

The fragmentation of the media, with new forms, formats, and players continuing to mushroom, gives political actors more opportunities for narrowcasting—that is, reaching particular audiences with more precision than was previously possible. This was in evidence during the 2024 campaign, when Trump and then Kamala Harris devoted precious time to appearing on podcasts that they surely did not listen to and perhaps had not previously heard of. But narrowcasting, by its nature, seems less available to incumbents than to challengers. If a president says something notable, what happens on the podcast is not likely to stay there.

[Jonathan Chait: Trump’s attacks on the media are self-defeating]

Although the president can take advantage of his unique ability to broadcast a message to virtually the whole nation, broadcasting is becoming less effective. In the last four decades of the 20th century, an address televised in prime time was a powerful tool, especially for presidents skilled at using the medium, including John F. Kennedy, Ronald Reagan, and Bill Clinton. Since the Obama administration, a president who appears on “all of the networks” is far from appearing on all of the screens. Even as the national population has grown by about a third since Reagan’s presidency, audiences for Trump’s State of the Union speeches, for instance, have been markedly smaller than the audiences in the 1980s. Much of what would previously have been the president’s audience is occupied elsewhere, streaming or scrolling, and often focused on matters other than public affairs. A larger share of voters today receives the president’s message only after it has been mediated by reporters, commentators, or social-media users. This would have been a significant detriment to the likes of Franklin D. Roosevelt, JFK, or Reagan.

Trump uses social media to powerful and unprecedented effect; it is the vehicle that he turns to, more than any other, to redirect the national conversation, often employing it to announce major policy and personnel moves. Still, social media is a deeply imperfect substitute for what TV used to be, from the perspective of presidential power. First, the short-form nature of social media encourages messages that are telegraphic rather than educational, making it an instrument of announcement more than persuasion. Second, social media makes it very easy for the people sharing messages to also interpret them. Not only has intermediation, long a frustration of presidents, increased, but far fewer of the mediators are journalists.

All of this has likely weakened the president’s once-celebrated ability to “teach” the country, in the manner of FDR during his fireside chats. For his February 1942 chat, about the tough early days of World War II, Roosevelt asked Americans to consult a map of the world as they listened. A president seeking to do this kind of teaching today would find that the “pupils” he most wanted to reach were those least likely to tune in, and that his “lessons” were being filtered and colored for many recipients (and by many). An exception to this trend may exist for moments of genuine crisis, but presidents must seize the occasion and be disciplined in doing so. Trump’s daily appearances during the coronavirus pandemic in March and April 2020, which unraveled quickly and then were discontinued, show how easily such a moment can be squandered.

One countervailing force is that when the press, particularly cable television, becomes more partisan, media actors can command loyalty to the president by intimidating other officials in his party into supporting him and his policies. Right-leaning media outlets have certainly helped Trump dominate Republican primary elections. But the same phenomenon all but guarantees a permanent opposition faction in the press, which can at times be just as strong as the supportive faction, if not more so. A partisan press also sharply limits a president’s ability to forge consensus, or even to seek compromise, which he needs in order to legislate with lasting effect.

[Read: The press is not the root of Trump’s problems]

One of the most profound ways that the news business has changed in this century is the nationalization of much of what passes for news, despite how deeply Americans still care about what’s happening in their local communities. Simply put, less local news is being produced, more local events are going unobserved, and national news often fills the void. Members of Congress who might once have heard at town halls about primarily district-level matters now find themselves buffeted by countrywide worries. For presidents, this seems, at best, a mixed blessing. When a president has events moving in his favor, the effect may be strengthened at the local level. Yet this same dynamic can exaggerate the effect when voters are unhappy with the state of the country—a secular trend at least in the past decade or more.

Finally, there is the often-noted decline in a shared set of facts. Public ignorance has been a challenge for all modern presidents. The proliferation of misinformation, and the microtargeting of that misinformation through social media, has created something worse: public misunderstanding of the facts. The current president, and those acting on his behalf or even at his behest, has exacerbated this problem by resorting to disinformation, a polite word for “lying.” Partisan news outlets are only too happy to amplify such messages. But over the long term, this creates a challenge for the president that is getting harder to confront. Public skepticism is on the rise. People are less inclined to believe even what they might see with their own eyes. This may well account for why, at least to date, Americans have not been overwhelmed with deepfakes, as some expected would come to pass. It also means that fact-based arguments can be more difficult for presidents to make.

There is something that presidential communications, even at their best, can’t spin: Americans’ day-to-day reality—the price of groceries, whether health care is available and affordable, news that a relative or friend has lost a job, the quality and price of housing. Americans seem to be living through the third successive failed presidential term—something that, by my judgment, has not occurred since the 19th century. The news environment might have made it harder for Joe Biden and Trump to get their messages out. But Biden’s foundering and Trump’s current political difficulties have more to do with the fact that both men seem to not understand how Americans feel about their lives. They can’t blame the press for that.

This article has been adapted from a chapter in the revised edition of Guardian of the Presidency: The Legacy of Richard E. Neustadt, forthcoming from Bloomsbury and the Brookings Institution Press.

content:
Fighting escalates after Tigrayan rebels form new coalition aimed at overthrowing Abiy Ahmed government

There are growing fears of a return to civil war in Ethiopia after an offensive by fighters from Tigray into the neighbouring states of Afar and Amhara and the formation of a new rebel alliance aimed at overthrowing the government of the prime minister, Abiy Ahmed.

About 600,000 people died between 2020 and 2022 during a devastating war between the Ethiopian army and the political party and paramilitary group the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). Both sides are now accusing the other of triggering a return to open conflict.
